name: invert_match
title: Switch location of matches to location of non-matches

origin.description: Turn a matrix of match locations into the locations of the stretches that were not matched.

arguments.name: loc
arguments.text: Matrix of match locations, as from str_locate_all, with columns start and end.

origin.details: start is c(0, end + 1) and end is c(start - 1, -1). An empty location matrix becomes the single row 0, -1. A missing position stays missing. The result has one more row than loc.
origin.value: An integer matrix with columns start and end giving the locations of the non-matches.
origin.example:
numbers <- "1 and 2 and 4 and 456"
num_loc <- str_locate_all(numbers, "[0-9]+")[[1]]
invert_match(num_loc)

translation.description: Turn match locations into the locations of the stretches that were not matched.

arguments.name: loc
arguments.text: A list of [start, end] rows, a list of {start, end} rows, or a dict with start and end columns. This is one element of str_locate_all.

translation.details: start is c(0, end + 1) and end is c(start - 1, -1), the same cbind as the R function. An empty list becomes [[0, -1]]. A missing position is stringi._na.NA and stays missing under the shift. The result has one more row than loc.
translation.value: A list of [start, end] rows. The same numbers R returns, including the leading 0 and the final -1.
translation.example:
from stringr.locate import invert_match, str_locate_all
numbers = "1 and 2 and 4 and 456"
num_loc = str_locate_all(numbers, "[0-9]+")[0]
print(invert_match(num_loc))
